newsitem.title: USA: INSTANT VIEW - US retail sales rise 0.2 pct in Oct.
newsitem.headline: INSTANT VIEW - US retail sales rise 0.2 pct in Oct.

text.p: Following are comments from U.S. economists after the Commerce Department said retail sales rose 0.2 percent in October, down from a revised 0.8 percent in the prior month.
Excluding automobiles, retail sales rose 0.4 percent.
Experts had expected a 0.3-percent increase in the overall rate and a 0.3-percent rise excluding autos.
CHERYL KATS, SENIOR ECONOMIST, MERRILL LYNCH: "The total retail sales number was a little bit less than what people were looking for."
"But you had revisions for the prior month so to offsetting it. It tells you the story that the consumer sector is turning off very mildly for the fourth quarter."
ASTRID ADOLFSON, SENIOR ECONOMIST, MCM MONEYWATCH INC: "Retail sales (had a) slight upward revision for the prior month, but it still shows sluggish growth (in consumer spending)."
Speaking about the 0.3 percent decline in auto sales, Adolfson said "it was expected, based on the unit sales that were released by the manufacturers."

WILLIAM GRIGGS, MANAGING DIRECTOR, GRIGGS & SANTOW INC: "The numbers this morning were a moderate plus for the market, but the market has run an awful long way and may find this not definitive enough to go any further."

Griggs continued: "Retail sales shows the economy does appear to be slowing down after a not spectacular third quarter. It's saying we're probably looking at another unspectacular fourth quarter, with the consumer being a little cautious and growth about 2.0 to 2.5 percent.

DAVID SLOAN, SENIOR ECONOMIST AT I.D.E.A. INC: "The numbers showed modest growth in consumer spending. The breakdown was mixed. We saw gains in general merchandise and food but weakness in autos and furniture.
"There's no real evidence yet of a pickup in consumer spending in Q4. But the information we're getting is that November should be a firmer month than October."

MARILYN SCHAJA, ECONOMIST AT DLJ: "The ex-auto number up 0.4 which is right on consensus and fits with the expected pattern of retail sales. It means retail sales is not that strong and suggests consumer spending is slowing."
